content: Red wine headache (RWH) is a condition characterized by a severe headache, often accompanied by nausea and facial flushing, that occurs in some individuals after consuming even a single glass of red wine. This reaction can sometimes develop within 15 minutes of drinking the wine. Interestingly, this phenomenon does not occur with white wine or other alcoholic beverages. Some individuals report experiencing a migraine-like headache hours after drinking certain red wines. The exact cause of RWH remains unknown, and it is likely that multiple factors contribute to this condition. Sulfites Sulfites, which are commonly found in wine, have been suspected as a cause of RWH due to the warning labels on wine bottles. However, this is unlikely to be the case. Nearly all wines contain sulfites, and sweet white wines often have higher sulfite levels than red wines. Additionally, dried fruits and processed foods, such as lunch meats, contain significantly more sulfites than red wine. Only a very small percentage of the population (less than 1%) is sensitive to sulfites, making it an improbable cause of RWH. Histamines Histamines are another potential cause of RWH, but they are likely responsible only in rare cases. Red wine contains 20-200% more histamines than white wine. Individuals who are sensitive to histamines often have a deficiency in a specific enzyme required to break them down. Some experts suggest that the combination of alcohol and this enzyme deficiency could trigger headaches. However, a study published in the Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology in February 2001 found no significant difference in reactions to wines with low versus high histamine levels among 16 individuals with red wine intolerance. Taking an antihistamine such as loratadine (Claritin) an hour before drinking red wine may help reduce histamine-related symptoms. This approach can help determine whether histamines are the cause of an individual's reaction. Another proposed solution is to drink black tea before consuming red wine, as it may have antihistamine effects. If histamines are not the cause, neither loratadine nor black tea will alleviate the symptoms. Tannins Tannins, which are flavonoids found in wine, are another suspected cause of RWH. These compounds contribute to the wine's mouth-drying bitterness and distinct taste, similar to the sensation of biting into a grape skin. Tannins are derived from grape skins, stems, and seeds, and red wines typically have higher tannin levels than white wines because they are fermented in contact with these components. Tannins can also be introduced from the oak barrels used for wine storage, with different types of wood imparting varying tannin profiles. Tannins play a role in preventing oxidation, which is important for a wine's aging potential. As red wines age, tannin molecules gradually precipitate out of the wine, forming harmless sediment. Certain wine styles, such as French reds from Bordeaux and Italian reds like Barolo and Barbaresco, are particularly tannic. In contrast, wines like Beaujolais, Tempranillo, and those made from Pinot Noir or Sangiovese grapes are lower in tannins. Tannins have been shown in well-controlled experiments to trigger the release of serotonin, a neurotransmitter. High levels of serotonin can cause headaches, particularly in individuals prone to migraines. However, this does not explain why people without a history of migraines also experience RWH. Additionally, tannins are present in other foods and beverages, such as tea, soy, and chocolate, yet these do not commonly cause headaches. Prostaglandins Another hypothesis is that RWH may be caused by the release of prostaglandins, substances that contribute to pain and inflammation. Some individuals may have difficulty metabolizing prostaglandins. Medications like ibuprofen (Advil) and aspirin, which are prostaglandin inhibitors, have been reported to help some people when taken an hour before consuming red wine. Yeast or Bacteria It has also been suggested that a specific strain of yeast or bacteria present in red wine could be responsible for RWH. However, this theory remains speculative and requires further investigation.
